findings.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:310 — [P1 confidence 100] "s.initErr = s.initWatcher()" — Starting the backend watch only after the full search rebuild snapshots the SQL watch cursor after that rebuild, so writes committed by another replica during the rebuild are permanently absent from the broadcaster for clients using an earlier Since value; delaying service availability does not preserve a watch contract that explicitly supports historical cursors.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:138 — [P1 confidence 100] "b.cache[key] = idx" — Publishing only after an uncoordinated build makes the GetIndex/BuildIndex split a non-atomic check-then-act, so concurrent misses for one memory-backed key each perform an O(N) rebuild and an older build completing last replaces an index that already received newer watch updates; keyed singleflight preserves cross-key parallelism without this data loss.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:261 — [P2 confidence 100] "return nil, err" — A failure after lifecycle initialization or search-watch startup discards the only server handle without calling Stop or cancel, leaving partially initialized backend and watcher resources with no owner; constructor-local rollback is required because a caller cannot clean up a nil result.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — [P1 confidence 100] "err := s.Init(ctx)" — Eager initialization does not replace the deleted per-RPC lifecycle-state checks, so after Stop records the stopped state every RPC except Watch continues into stopped dependencies instead of rejecting the call.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — [P1 confidence 100] "b.cacheMu.Lock()" — Locking only publication leaves same-key cache misses unsynchronized, so simultaneous misses build separate indexes and the later publication discards every update accepted by the first index between the two publications.

goldens.comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:310 — [P1 confidence 100] "s.initErr = s.initWatcher()" — Starting the backend watch only after the full search rebuild snapshots the SQL watch cursor after that rebuild, so writes committed by another replica during the rebuild are permanently absent from the broadcaster for clients using an earlier Since value; delaying service availability does not preserve a watch contract that explicitly supports historical cursors.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the order of initialization was changed: previously initWatcher() was called before s.search.init(ctx), now it's called after. The finding correctly identifies that this reordering means the SQL watch cursor is established after the search index rebuild completes. If writes occur during the rebuild (which can take significant time as shown by the new log 'search index initialized' with duration_secs), those writes would be committed to the database but the watch cursor would be positioned after them. The watch contract supporting historical 'Since' values means clients could request events from before the cursor position that would never be delivered. This is a real correctness issue with the initialization order change.

If Init() succeeds but returns an error later (or if there's a partial initialization), the server 's' has already been created with resources like backend connections, tracers, and potentially started watchers. The server struct 's' goes out of scope without proper cleanup of its initialized resources. This is a valid resource leak concern - the backend, search support, and other components may have been partially initialized but are never cleaned up on error paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — [P1 confidence 100] "b.cacheMu.Lock()" — Locking only publication leaves same-key cache misses unsynchronized, so simultaneous misses build separate indexes and the later publication discards every update accepted by the first index between the two publications.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the lock was moved from the beginning of BuildIndex to just before cache insertion (lines 137-139). This means if two goroutines call BuildIndex for the same key simultaneously, both will proceed to build separate indexes in parallel (no lock protecting the build phase), and when they both try to insert into the cache, the second one will overwrite the first. Any updates that were applied to the first index between the two publications would be lost. This is a real race condition introduced by moving the lock.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — [P1 confidence 100] "err := s.Init(ctx)" — The constructor now performs the entire blocking database and search-index initialization on a background-derived context whose cancel function is inaccessible until the constructor returns, so a stuck backend or index build makes startup uninterruptibly hang.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that s.Init(ctx) is now called directly in NewResourceServer at line 258, where ctx comes from opts.Lifecycle.Context (line 188). Looking at the Init method, it performs blocking operations including s.search.init(ctx) which initializes the search index. The finding correctly identifies that if these operations hang, there's no way to cancel them since the context's cancel function isn't exposed until after the constructor returns. This is a real architectural issue - moving initialization from lazy (per-request) to eager (constructor) without proper timeout/cancellation handling could cause startup hangs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:98 — [P1 confidence 100] "index, err = bleve.New(dir, mapper)" — Removing the build-wide cache lock lets concurrent first builds for the same disk-backed key call bleve.New on the identical must-not-exist path, so one request deterministically fails with ErrorIndexPathExists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the cache lock (b.cacheMu.Lock/Unlock) being moved from the beginning of BuildIndex to after the index is built, just before adding to cache. This means concurrent calls to BuildIndex for the same key can both proceed past the initial check and both attempt to create a new bleve index. For disk-backed indexes (when size > b.opts.FileThreshold), both calls would try to call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the same directory path. Since bleve.New creates a new index at that path and fails if it already exists, one of the concurrent calls would fail with an error. This is a real race condition bug introduced by moving the lock.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — [P1 confidence 100] "err := s.Init(ctx)" — works today, breaks when lifecycle initialization, search-index I/O, or watcher setup stalls because NewResourceServer then waits forever under a context with no deadline whose cancellation function is trapped in the not-yet-returned server.

Looking at the Init method, it performs search.init(ctx) and initWatcher() operations. The context passed is created at line 213 with context.Background() and has no deadline. If Init blocks indefinitely (e.g., search index I/O stalls), NewResourceServer will never return, and the caller has no way to cancel or timeout the operation since the context has no deadline and the server (with any cancellation mechanisms) hasn't been returned yet. This is a legitimate concern about blocking initialization without timeout protection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — [P1 confidence 100] "b.cacheMu.Lock()" — works today, breaks when a burst of searches hits uncached resources because the lock is acquired only after every request has independently scanned storage and built an index, permitting one simultaneous full-index build per request until database and memory capacity are exhausted.

This means multiple concurrent requests for the same uncached resource can each independently build a full index before any of them acquires the lock to store it in the cache. This is a real concurrency bug that could cause redundant expensive index builds and memory pressure under load.
